name: d-glob-py
summary: Task C in Python, function for function and case for case. The control for ADR-0062's floor of twelve, which was measured entirely against a Rust compiler.
tests_at: top-level functions named `test_{module}_<what it checks>` at the end of the file

slices.implement: `split_segs` is unimplemented. Implement it so its tests pass.
slices.specify: `split_segs(path) -> list[str]` splits a path on '/' and drops empty components, so "a//b" and "/a/b/" both give ["a", "b"] and "" gives [].

slices.signature: def match_seg(pattern: str, component: str) -> bool:
slices.implement: `match_seg` is unimplemented. Implement it so its tests pass. It matches ONE path component against one pattern segment, where `*` is any run of characters and `?` is exactly one.
slices.specify: `match_seg(pattern, component) -> bool` matches ONE path component against one pattern segment. `*` matches any run of characters, including none; `?` matches exactly one. Neither matches a '/'.

slices.signature: def glob_match(pattern: str, path: str) -> bool:
slices.implement: `glob_match` is unimplemented. Implement it so its tests pass. `**` crosses `/`, `*` and `?` do not.
slices.specify: `glob_match(pattern, path) -> bool` matches a whole glob pattern against a whole path. `**` matches any number of path components including none; `*` and `?` stay inside one component, where `*` is any run of characters and `?` is exactly one.

slices.signature: def classify(classes: list[FileClass], path: str) -> str | None:
slices.implement: `classify` is unimplemented. Implement it so its tests pass. The first class whose include globs match wins.
slices.specify: `classify(classes, path) -> str | None` returns the name of the first class in the list whose include globs match the path, or None.
